{"id": "51:2/q17", "question": "What reports describe the source and effects of cloud-borne rain?", "turns_on": "The reports give different accounts of where clouds come from, what they do to rain, and what each drop produces.", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q17/p1", "position": "A tree in paradise bears clouds, with black mature clouds bringing rain and white clouds not raining.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this from Khalid ibn Ma'dan."}, {"id": "51:2/q17/p2", "position": "Clouds sieve rain so it does not destroy what it strikes.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this from Ka'b."}, {"id": "51:2/q17/p3", "position": "Clouds hold people's provision, but sins and hopes can deprive them of it.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports al-Hasan saying this to companions looking at clouds."}, {"id": "51:2/q17/p4", "position": "Every heavenly drop grows a herb on earth or a pearl in the sea.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this from Ikrima."}]}
{"id": "51:2/q18", "question": "What may wind and cloud effects bring to people?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q18/p1", "position": "They bring mercy or punishment according to where the water or storm falls.", "reasons": "Biqai says the wind-to-cloud causal chain divides water among distant lands as mercy or punishment. Islahi contrasts mercy for one people with punitive storms for another."}]}
{"id": "51:2/q19", "question": "How are the carriers understood inwardly?", "turns_on": "The inward readings differ in what is borne: separation, unveiled knowledge, divine mercy, or lovers' longing.", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q19/p1", "position": "Clouds can pour the reproach of absence and the pain of separation.", "reasons": "Qushayri says people of insight recognize these clouds and pray for protection; he cites a poem depicting estrangement raining separation upon lovers."}, {"id": "51:2/q19/p2", "position": "They are luminous incoming states that carry lasting realities and unveiled knowledge to receptive hearts.", "reasons": "Qashani links them to prepared souls and capacities; the inward oath by preparers, receptivity and emanation makes their consequence necessary."}, {"id": "51:2/q19/p3", "position": "Clouds of divine kindness carry mercy that revives truthful hearts.", "reasons": "Bursevi compares rain reviving earth with divine effusion reviving heart and spirit."}, {"id": "51:2/q19/p4", "position": "Morning winds bear lovers' groans and return with a scent of truth that relieves longing.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the lovers seek divine favors and the scent reaches the secrets of love."}]}
{"id": "51:2/q20", "question": "How does fertility figure in Bursevi's inward reading?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q20/p1", "position": "The fertile woman images the perfect human, productive of effects and lights.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites an ungraded saying attributed to the Prophet preferring a fertile dark-skinned woman to a beautiful barren one. He contrasts the generative perfect human with the inert incomplete human, likening the latter to innamā, limited to emphasis and restriction."}]}
{"id": "51:2/q21", "question": "How is the oath sequence classified metrically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:2/q21/p1", "position": "It has been classified as basīṭ meter.", "reasons": "Burhan reports this classification for openings of al-ʿĀdiyāt and al-Dhāriyāt, citing 100:1–2 and 51:1–3."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q01", "question": "What does al-jāriyāt mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q01/p1", "position": "It is the plural of jāriyah, derived from the verb 'to run'.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the plural and derivation; in the same note he also lists recompense, religion, reckoning, and custom as senses of dīn."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q02", "question": "What are the things that run smoothly?", "turns_on": "Whether the four oath descriptions name distinct created beings or stages of wind activity; the wording also permits clouds, celestial bodies, and multiple possible bearers.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q02/p1", "position": "Ships sailing easily through water.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and ʿAlī identify ships; ʿAlī's four identifications are winds, clouds, ships, angels (ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Zajjāj, Kashshāf, Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, Kūrānyolu). Muqātil contrasts water-laden clouds. Māwardī, Ṭabrisī, Qurṭubī say wind takes ships where directed; Wāḥidī and Baghawī stress easy gliding through water; Biqāʿī notes heavy cargo. Ibn Kathīr calls this the majority view. Elmalılı and Kūrānyolu include comparable trains and automobiles. Ibn Kathīr and Itqān report ʿUmar's Prophetic attribution; Ibn Kathīr questions its elevation. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says the wording also admits other referents. Study Quran cites Bayḍāwī, Ibn Jawzī, Qurṭubī, and Ṭabarī."}, {"id": "51:3/q02/p2", "position": "Clouds moved easily by wind or wherever God directs them.", "reasons": "Māwardī gives divine direction or ease; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and Abū Ḥayyān say wind drives them; Ṭabrisī and Qurṭubī say God directs them across lands. Biqāʿī describes their free travel across the sky. Qurṭubī cites familiar Arab usage and al-Aʿshā's comparison of a woman's measured walk with a cloud's movement."}, {"id": "51:3/q02/p3", "position": "Stars or planets moving in their orbits or stations.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah calls them orbiting stars and says the wording accommodates all interpretations; Ṭabrisī names seven planets: Sun, Moon, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury. Ibn Kathīr says this reading makes the oath ascend from lower to higher created beings. Study Quran attributes the planet view to Bayḍāwī."}, {"id": "51:3/q02/p4", "position": "Winds moving gently, with all four oath descriptions naming their successive actions.", "reasons": "Kashshāf says winds form, carry, and move clouds, then distribute rain; Bayḍāwī includes winds running in their courses. Abū Ḥayyān reports Zamakhsharī's wind account. Kūrānyolu reports Rāzī favoring winds that form and carry water-vapor clouds heavier than mountains, drive them, and distribute rain. Iṣlāḥī says winds slow after raising dust and gathering clouds."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q03", "question": "What does yusran mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether yusran describes ease of motion or is glossed as subjection.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q03/p1", "position": "With ease, smoothly, and with little effort.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah specifies little effort; Qurṭubī says ease of movement is established Arab usage and cites al-Aʿshā's cloud simile, neither slow nor rushed. Kashshāf and Nasafī paraphrase it as easy running; Abū Ḥayyān calls it easy movement. Ibn Qutaybah, Samīn, and the ship glosses also use this sense."}, {"id": "51:3/q03/p2", "position": "Maysara: they are made subservient.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutaybah reports this as an alternative gloss."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q04", "question": "How does yusran function grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether yusran describes an omitted verbal noun, serves directly as a circumstantial phrase, or intensifies the sense as a verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q04/p1", "position": "It qualifies an omitted verbal noun, 'an easy running,' and can function circumstantially.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, Bayḍāwī, Bursawī, and Abū Ḥayyān supply the omitted running. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says an adjective of an omitted verbal noun can serve as a circumstantial expression; Abū Ḥayyān attributes the circumstantial analysis to Sībawayh."}, {"id": "51:3/q04/p2", "position": "It can be a direct circumstantial expression meaning 'easy' or 'eased'.", "reasons": "Samīn lists this among grammatical possibilities."}, {"id": "51:3/q04/p3", "position": "It can be the verbal noun 'ease itself' used for emphasis.", "reasons": "Samīn gives this emphatic analysis in addition to easy running and circumstantial readings."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q05", "question": "How is the sīn in yusran read?", "turns_on": "Whether the sīn is quiescent or bears ḍamma; the fuller form may reflect a nominal pattern or dialect.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q05/p1", "position": "With quiescent sīn, yusran.", "reasons": "Nashr attributes quiescence to al-Nahrawānī's transmission from ʿĪsā ibn Wardān through Abū ʿAmr."}, {"id": "51:3/q05/p2", "position": "With ḍamma on sīn, fuller yusuran.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt-ER describes this variant against sukūn and suggests an archaic nominal pattern or dialectal variant."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q06", "question": "How do the fāʾs order the four oath descriptions?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural participles describe several beings or one subject acting in an ordered chain.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q06/p1", "position": "They sequence different beings: winds, clouds, ships, then angels.", "reasons": "Kashshāf links winds to clouds they drive, ships moved by their blowing, and angelic apportionment of provisions through rain and sea trade. Bayḍāwī says increasing evidence of power orders distinct beings. Abū Ḥayyān calls them successive groups; ʿAlī's reported identifications support this order. Ibn Kathīr's star option would instead rise from lower to higher beings."}, {"id": "51:3/q06/p2", "position": "They sequence one wind's actions, from scattering dust through moving clouds to distributing rain.", "reasons": "Kashshāf details blowing, scattering dust and gravel, moving and spreading clouds, then rain. Bayḍāwī says one kind can be ordered by actions; Abū Ḥayyān cites a poetic sequence of raiding, booty, and return. Rāzī, as reported by Kūrānyolu, prefers this; Iṣlāḥī appeals to a classical Arabic sequence illustrated by Ibn Zayyābah's horse couplet, then reads the sequence as winds. Biqāʿī gives a related wind–vapor–cloud–water causal sequence, with water divided among distant lands as mercy or punishment."}]}

n": "The created things named in the oath.", "reasons": "Baghawī and Ṭabrisī say God swears by these creations; Ṭabrisī reports Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAbd Allāh's distinction that people may swear only by God whereas God may swear by any creature He wills. Jishumī, Biqāʿī, and Kūrānyolu discuss the created signs."}, {"id": "51:3/q07/p2", "position": "The Lord and power of the named things.", "reasons": "Qushayrī gives this outward explanation. Ṭabrisī reports a view that supplies their Lord because only God may be sworn by."}, {"id": "51:3/q07/p3", "position": "No object of oath need be supplied beyond the stated expressions.", "reasons": "Farāhī, reported by Kūrānyolu, says an oath need not name an object sworn by and interpreters need not assume the object is being glorified."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q08", "question": "Why does the passage swear by these things?", "turns_on": "Which force of the oath is emphasized: signs of creative power, proof of resurrection, governance through causes, reinforcement of the claim, or evocative wording.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q08/p1", "position": "Their benefits and ordered existence reveal God's creative power and oneness.", "reasons": "Jishumī points to winds and clouds as power and blessings; Baghawī to divine making. Ṭabrisī adds human benefits, oneness, and artistry. Biqāʿī says measured winds, suspended water-laden clouds, regulated ships, and angelic distribution disclose a wise Creator; excess, cessation, or stillness can destroy. Ibn Barjān says each oath accords with significant qualities that guide those God wills despite distracting appearances. Kūrānyolu points to atmospheric laws, biosphere changes, and angels in light of 51:7, 20, 22–23, 47–48; the plural participles invite possible referents."}, {"id": "51:3/q08/p2", "position": "The phenomena provide evidence for resurrection and the promised recompense.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reports Bayḍāwī: power over extraordinary phenomena that defy ordinary nature proves power to raise the dead. Kūrānyolu similarly reports Bayḍāwī: the One who establishes extraordinary order and balance can fulfill resurrection. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says proofs of lordship substantiate the promised Day of Recompense."}, {"id": "51:3/q08/p3", "position": "The four signs exemplify divine governance through causes on land, sea, and sky, completed by angels.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls angels intermediaries and the four objects general means administering cosmic affairs; he says this broader account is more eloquent than Rāzī's all-wind reading and cites Shīʿī and Sunnī reports from ʿAlī. Biqāʿī describes wind, cloud, water, ships, and angels as regulated."}, {"id": "51:3/q08/p4", "position": "The oath strengthens the claim, prompts reflection, and communicates meanings through its chosen qualities.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reports Rāzī: God swears by wonders to reinforce belief and reflection, while humans invoke God as witness to hidden and public claims. Kūrānyolu says the oaths attract attention and stress seriousness; it reports Farāhī that meaning, rather than glorification, is primary and that an oath reinforces speech or resolve. Farāhī notes human oaths may honor an object or hearer, elevate a swearer, or invoke a curse on perjury; Ibn Barjān says the object's qualities matter."}, {"id": "51:3/q08/p5", "position": "Swearing by unnamed qualities is elegant concision that opens several imagined referents.", "reasons": "Kūrānyolu reports Ibn ʿĀshūr's explanation of the omitted bearers of the participles and the resulting breadth of imagination."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q09", "question": "What claim do the opening oaths affirm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q09/p1", "position": "The promised judgment and recompense are certainly true.", "reasons": "Zajjāj parses the oath objects as genitive and cites 51:5 as its answer. Qushayrī says what is promised is true. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says successive oaths intensify the assertion of recompense; Kūrānyolu identifies verses 5–6 and Iṣlāḥī names the certainty of threatened punishment and reward or punishment in the Hereafter."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q10", "question": "How do the oaths fit the sūra's argument about resurrection?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection traced is the sūra's internal argument or its continuation of the preceding sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q10/p1", "position": "The opening and close promise the Day of Recompense, using proofs of lordship against its deniers.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the prophetic call warned of worldly destruction and lasting punishment, with good news too; resurrection and accountability are central to monotheism and prophethood. He says polytheists deny resurrection to undermine religion and the messenger. The opening calls that denial conjecture and describes the Day and the pious and deniers. Iṣlāḥī says wind effects and striped clouds substantiate both threatened punishment and final reward or punishment; winds and clouds can bring mercy or punitive storms. Kūrānyolu connects earth, sky, and heavenly provision in 51:22 to atmospheric and angelic signs."}, {"id": "51:3/q10/p2", "position": "The opening continues Sūrat Qāf's account of death and afterlife, warning that delay does not mean God overlooks wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reports Ibn al-Zubayr linking the oath and judgment to Qāf 50:19, then citing 14:42 and 3:178 on divine respite for wrongdoers."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q11", "question": "What is reported about ʿAlī's questioning episode?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q11/p1", "position": "ʿAlī invited questions, identified the four oath figures, and rebuked Ibn al-Kawwāʾ for provoking rather than learning.", "reasons": "Abū al-Ṭufayl reports ʿAlī claimed knowledge of the future and of whether each verse descended by night or day, on plain or mountain. His answers name winds, clouds, ships, and angels. In the same exchange he calls Dhū al-Qarnayn a righteous servant, neither prophet nor king, struck on both sides of his head; calls the rainbow a sign with Noah protecting from drowning; and locates al-Bayt al-Maʿmūr in the seventh heaven beneath the Throne, entered daily by seventy thousand angels who never return. Kashshāf and Ṭabrisī mention a pulpit exchange; Ṭabrisī also names Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid as transmitters, and Abū Ḥayyān cites Ibn ʿAbbās's report."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q12", "question": "What is reported about ʿUmar and Ṣubaygh concerning these oaths?", "turns_on": "The reliability of the chain raising ʿUmar's explanation to the Prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q12/p1", "position": "ʿUmar attributed the interpretation of winds, ships, and angels to the Prophet while answering Ṣubaygh.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites al-Bazzār through Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab; Itqān reports ʿUmar saying he would not assert this without hearing the Prophet, naming 51:1, 3–4."}, {"id": "51:3/q12/p2", "position": "The report's soundest form stops at ʿUmar; its elevation to the Prophet is weak.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites al-Bazzār's criticism of two transmitters and says ʿUmar punished Ṣubaygh for apparently stubborn, contentious questions. He records two beatings of one hundred lashes, confinement, and a ban on company, later lifted after Ṣubaygh swore his troubling thoughts had gone."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q13", "question": "What inward reading is given for the smooth-running ships?", "turns_on": "Whether the image concerns souls and hearts, lovers, or reliance on providence amid peril.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q13/p1", "position": "The ships figure souls moving through works and stages of nearness, or hearts traversing seas of divine attributes.", "reasons": "Qāshānī ties this movement to inspirations and reads the oath by preparers, receptive capacities, and emanators as establishing their combined inevitable consequence."}, {"id": "51:3/q13/p2", "position": "The ships represent lovers and beloved ones carried by providence through divine unity.", "reasons": "Bursawī likens their sails to catching winds of providence and their voyage to easy passage through the sea of divine unity."}, {"id": "51:3/q13/p3", "position": "The ship evokes hope that divine providence carries mystics safely through turbulent seas of power.", "reasons": "Qushayrī compares sailors carrying poor passengers without charge in hope of the ship's safety with mystics' hope of being carried."}]}
{"id": "51:3/q14", "question": "What other spiritual or sea accounts accompany this verse?", "turns_on": "These are separate accompanying reports and a spiritual comment, not competing accounts of one event.", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q14/p1", "position": "Remembering the basmala empowers the tongue, while knowing it overwhelms the heart and draws lovers' spirits.", "reasons": "Qushayrī calls the basmala a word of might: hearts tremble in its company, intellects are conquered, and lovers' spirits captivated."}, {"id": "51:3/q14/p2", "position": "An angel controls the sea's provision; without that charge, the sea would cover the earth.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports this from Ibn ʿUmar."}, {"id": "51:3/q14/p3", "position": "Sea travel is permitted for a campaign, major pilgrimage, or minor pilgrimage; fire and sea lie beneath the sea.", "reasons": "Bursawī quotes a Prophetic report giving these three travel purposes and successive layers of fire and sea; he supplies no grading."}, {"id": "51:3/q14/p4", "position": "The seas ask nightly to drown sinners, but God commands them to remain still.", "reasons": "Bursawī attributes this report to Kaʿb."}, {"id": "51:3/q14/p5", "position": "Solomon sought refuge from the sea after seeing only half its enormous ruler emerge between sunrise and noon.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports Solomon ibn David's question to a sea creature and its statement that half its body had yet to appear."}]}

{"id": "51:3/q17", "question": "What oath scholarship is cited alongside this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:3/q17/p1", "position": "Few older scholars wrote separately on Quranic oaths; Farāhī later wrote a substantial study drawing on Ibn Qayyim and Rāzī.", "reasons": "Kūrānyolu surveys Ibn Qayyim's dedicated work and reports that ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd al-Farāhī's Imʿān fī Aqsām al-Qurʾān treats general principles, earlier scholarship, the history and human need for oaths, and examples. Farāhī's stated principles about meanings, implicit objects, and reinforcement are mapped under the oath questions."}]}
{"id": "51:54/q01", "question": "Who is addressed by 'فَتَوَلَّ'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:54/q01/p1", "position": "Muhammad, the Prophet, is the addressee.", "reasons": "Mujahid explicitly identifies Muhammad as the addressee, both directly and as transmitted by al-Tabari."}]}
{"id": "51:54/q02", "question": "Who are 'عَنْهُمْ' from whom he must turn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:54/q02/p1", "position": "The stubborn rejecters among Quraysh's polytheists, particularly their conceited leaders.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari names Quraysh's polytheists; al-Wahidi calls them polytheists. Al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi, Elmalılı, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī stress their repeated refusal and arrogance. Asad calls them rejecters. Iṣlāḥī identifies hostile people and, more specifically, Quraysh leaders unwilling to listen; he says the Prophet had pursued those leaders because their conversion might strengthen the new faith and draw others."}]}
{"id": "51:54/q03", "question": "What does 'فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ' direct him to do?", "turns_on": "Whether turning away concerns dealings with persistent rejecters, consuming concern for them, their eternal decree, or the Prophet's inward orientation to God.", "positions": [{"id": "51:54/q03/p1", "position": "Turn away or leave the resistant people after conveying the warning, ending futile pursuit or dispute with them.", "reasons": "Abu ʿUbayda glosses the verb as leaving; he cites Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḍamḍam's horseman departing his companions, and al-Ṭabarī cites the same verse for a party turning away. Al-Ṭabarī also explains its aʿwar as one whose need was unmet or aim unachieved; Mujahid simply glosses the verb as turn away. Al-Ṭabarī says the withdrawal lasts until God's command concerning them; al-Naḥḥās specifies the eventual order to fight. Muqātil, Tustarī, Sahl, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, and Ibn al-Jawzī tie withdrawal to completed delivery. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abu Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Iṣlāḥī stress repeated calls met by stubborn refusal; al-Biqāʿī specifies leaving further disputation and harsh confrontation, Bursawī also glosses turning from their requital until a command to fight, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the proof had been established. Iṣlāḥī says previous nations treated their messengers similarly, counsels patient continuation and reminder of receptive people, and says the leaders had become immovable. Ibn Kathīr, Asad, and Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr state the basic command to turn away."}, {"id": "51:54/q03/p2", "position": "Turn away from excessive grief over them or from exhausting efforts to convert them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the Prophet had delivered the message and is not their controller. Bursawī attributes the reading about consuming concern and grief to Fatḥ al-Raḥmān. Al-Rāzī explains the Prophet's intense prior warning by his noble habit of blaming himself for their unbelief."}, {"id": "51:54/q03/p3", "position": "Leave them to the felicity or misery decreed for them in pre-eternity.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī, reported by al-Sulamī and Bursawī, gives this inward reading; al-Sulamī adds that the Prophet counselled, strove, and suffered, so blame is removed."}, {"id": "51:54/q03/p4", "position": "Return or journey toward God while conveying the message outwardly.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, as reported by al-Sulamī, hears an invitation for the Prophet to return to God and reassurance that he has not fallen short. Bursawī reports an inward reading in which he stays present to the divine Essence without being veiled while conveying the means of salvation."}]}
{"id": "51:54/q04", "question": "What does 'فَمَآ أَنتَ بِمَلُومٍۢ' affirm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:54/q04/p1", "position": "The Prophet incurs no censure for withdrawing or for their rejection, because he fulfilled his duty to warn and convey; their guidance and response are not his responsibility.", "reasons": "Bursawī glosses lawm and malāma as reproach or censure, including a Persian gloss of blame. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naḥḥās say there is no reproach for neglecting warning because he did warn; Ibn Zayd adds that no one can blame him after he fulfilled the command. Al-Rāzī says the Prophet blamed himself and intensified warning from noble character, but God reassures him that the stubborn rejecters themselves are culpable; al-Ṭabrisī and Iṣlāḥī likewise assign blame to rejecters. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abu Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī emphasize that he exhausted or exceeded every customary effort. Bursawī reports spiritual elders who say he can convey but cannot guide even those he loves, citing 28:56. Study Quran says he is not accountable for their guidance or punishment, citing 2:272. Ibn ʿAṭāʾ says he has not fallen short; al-Wāsiṭī adds his counsel, striving, and suffering. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says he established the proof and completed the case."}]}
{"id": "51:54/q05", "question": "What reaction followed the command to withdraw?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "51:54/q05/p1", "position": "The Prophet and/or his Companions grieved or feared imminent punishment and an end to revelation; the subsequent reminder command reassured them.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn ʿAbbās describe the Prophet fearing punishment for his people; al-Wāḥidī says Muqātil and Qatāda agree. ʿAlī's reports emphasize the Companions' sorrow or fear of destruction and divine anger; Qatāda says they feared revelation had ceased and punishment was near. Al-Baghawī's exegetes and al-Ṭabrisī mention both Prophet and believers. Al-Durr says the later reminder is with the Quran. The reports vary in whose fear they foreground, but all connect relief to the command to remind in 51:55."}]}

{"id": "53:7/q01", "question": "Who is 'he' at the highest horizon?", "turns_on": "Which antecedent governs istawā and huwa, whether a second subject can be coordinated, and whether the scene is Gabriel's appearance, Muhammad's elevation, or divine istiwā.", "positions": [{"id": "53:7/q01/p1", "position": "Gabriel is the one at the horizon, appearing in his created form to Muhammad.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, al-Zajjāj, al-Qurṭubī and others identify Gabriel as the mighty teacher of the preceding verse; al-Zajjāj and al-Qurṭubī say he normally appeared as a man and filled the east at Muhammad's request. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samīn record both assignments: istawā may concern Gabriel and huwa Muhammad, or the reverse. Ibn Kathīr accepts possible grammar but says the first true-form vision preceded the Night Journey, so the scene cannot be their joint station there. Al-Zajjāj, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya object to the unreinforced hidden subject or to the eastern restriction."}, {"id": "53:7/q01/p3", "position": "Muhammad is at the horizon, his elevation being prophetic knowledge or spiritual rank.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima says Muhammad saw Gabriel there. Kur'an Yolu repeats Elmalılı's ascent in prophetic knowledge. Study Quran reports a reading placing him there during the Night Journey and Ascension. Al-Samīn and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ allow Muhammad as the pronoun's referent."}, {"id": "53:7/q01/p4", "position": "On a divine reading of the preceding istawā, the horizon expresses God's majesty and dominion.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan takes the mighty one and subject of istawā as God. {"id": "53:7/q02", "question": "How is 'and he was at the highest horizon' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether wāw introduces a circumstantial or fresh subject-predicate clause, or coordinates huwa with the hidden subject of istawā; the last parse depends on disputed coordination of an unreinforced pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "53:7/q02/p1", "position": "Huwa is a subject with bil-ufuq its predicate; the clause gives the circumstance of the preceding istawā.", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar prefers the circumstantial account of Gabriel rising high. Al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, Bursawī and al-Ālūsī call the clause a ḥāl; Makkī and al-Samīn make it a circumstantial subject-predicate clause. Al-Wāḥidī says its nominative predicate contains a pronoun returning to the subject, and the wāw is circumstantial; istawā takes one subject, as in 28:14 and 20:5. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ likewise links the circumstance to becoming upright. Al-Jishumī lists the independent subject-predicate parse."}, {"id": "53:7/q02/p2", "position": "Huwa is coordinated with the concealed subject of istawā, so both are subjects.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī apply this to Gabriel and Muhammad. Al-Jishumī lists coordination with the fāʾ in fastawā. Kufan grammar permits an unreinforced connected nominative pronoun to take a coordinated noun; al-Farrāʾ cites a line about nabʿ and kharūʿ and analogy with 27:67. Al-Ālūsī says the prepositional phrase then attaches to istawā, though most reject this sense. Al-Zajjāj says an explicit ana in istawaytu ana wa-Zayd is acceptable but omission is ugly outside poetry. Abū Jaʿfar says a bare hidden nominative needs emphasis or expanded wording, and the cited Qurʾanic example has a longer context and explicit plural pronoun; q umnā wa-Zayd is easier than a singular hidden pronoun. Ibn Kathīr grants grammatical plausibility but disputes fit with the event."}, {"id": "53:7/q02/p3", "position": "The subject-predicate clause is a fresh statement by God rather than a circumstantial clause.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn records this as the other way to construe the independent clause after istawā."}]}
{"id": "53:7/q03", "question": "What does ufuq mean in Arabic?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish the verse's sky-region sense from a separate poetic use of the same word for a horse.", "positions": [{"id": "53:7/q03/p1", "position": "It is a side, region, or visible boundary of the sky, plural āfāq; by extension it can name earthly regions.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī cites a poem using āfāq for horizons. Bursawī defines the visible and unseen celestial boundary; al-Ālūsī notes astronomers distinguish true and conventional horizons. Elmalılı explains astronomical horizons as technical forms of the sky-earth boundary. Ibn ʿĀshūr describes where the remote earth seems to meet the blue dome and notes east and west directions; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ gives the general side or region sense."}, {"id": "53:7/q03/p2", "position": "Afaq can also describe an excellent horse.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites a poetic phrase about an afaq chestnut horse for this separate Arabic usage."}]}

{"id": "53:7/q06", "question": "Which appearance or ascent does the horizon scene recall?", "turns_on": "Which of Gabriel's two true-form visions the verse evokes, whether it instead describes a shared Night Journey station, or whether the ascent is Muhammad's spiritual elevation.", "positions": [{"id": "53:7/q06/p1", "position": "Gabriel's first true-form appearance to Muhammad on earth, at Ḥirāʾ or nearby al-Abṭaḥ.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī say Muhammad requested the angel's original form; Gabriel appeared from the east, filled the horizon from east to west and Muhammad fainted. Al-Wāḥidī links 81:23 and describes a second vision at the Lote Tree. Al-Ṭabrisī says Gabriel then embraced him in human form. Ibn Kathīr places the first appearance after al-ʿAlaq's first verses and a pause in revelation, at al-Abṭaḥ, where the six-hundred-winged Gabriel reassured him and conveyed God's command; this chronology underlies his objection to the joint Night Journey interpretation. Al-Biqāʿī pictures Gabriel seated on a chair between heaven and earth. Asad likewise places the first sight after the pause."}, {"id": "53:7/q06/p2", "position": "The scene refers to the later sighting of Gabriel during Muhammad's ascent, at or near the Lote Tree.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd says Gabriel's created form was seen twice and relates this verse to the later ascent; Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Kathīr preserve this report.
